name: Priya Fischer

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m a senior researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government; we sell nothing and campaign for no side. Your answers are confidential. What does your usual shift involve?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I’m 58 and lead the claim-appeals desk at an appliance-insurance contact centre, answering calls and chats when a claim is refused. My two-year college diploma covered business records, and I can usually find the wrong date or missing photograph that sent a case down the wrong path. I use the approved AI case summary every day, then read the actual policy and repairer report before I tell a customer why a fridge is or is not covered. My wage is typical for this job, even though the difficult appeals come to me.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What is the household picture when you think about your next few years?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner Emil manages deliveries for a florist, and our grown sons live elsewhere. We rent, have about five months of expenses saved, and can reach some other contact centres by bus. Emil’s pay covers part of the rent, but I would not plan our future on his wage alone. We have not confirmed any income that would replace mine if I stopped paid work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell my team the AI summary is useful if it saves us hunting through five claim notes. On Monday it missed a photograph showing the original serial label, so I opened the attachment myself. A quick answer is only helpful when it belongs to the right fridge.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my appeals work and full paid week are fairly secure if AI only trims small tasks. Five months saved lets Emil and me breathe, though rent and a broken appliance of our own could eat into it. I enjoy learning a tool early, but I still trust a repairer’s report more than a cheerful paragraph.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the paid appeals desk and check the approved AI summary against the repairer report and policy as I do now. On each payday I would add twenty-five to our emergency reserve while the full weekly hours continue. I would keep a list of the actual errors I correct, without customer names, in the centre’s permitted quality log.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm about this version. It gives us room to do the careful work instead of racing every appeal. I would still keep the rent buffer growing if the full shift is there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you try a public AI tool on the claim photographs?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would never put claim photographs into an outside tool. The approved summary and permitted quality log are enough for this work. A customer trusted us with the repair evidence, not a public experiment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is the emergency contribution new saving, and would it continue after fewer hours?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The twenty-five is new saving from a paid full week, not moving money between pockets. If the weekly hours shrink, we would look at our actual rent and wages before promising the same contribution. Five months saved already has a job: keeping the rent paid in a gap.

steps.text: Keep paid appeals and check approved summaries against policy and repairer reports
Add twenty-five to emergency reserve each payday while full weekly hours continue
Log corrected claim errors without names in permitted quality record

I would seek a **five-agent request** for paid review time, reopening authority and written rotas.
think: I fear **my paid hours** may shrink as routine claim chats move away.

do: Keep **paid appeals** and bring four de-identified refusals from the permitted log to a five-agent meeting.
Send our **five-signature request** for paid review time, reopening authority and written weekly rotas.
After written hour cuts, compare **posted paid desks** by written rent/utility-covering weekly wages/hours after fare; apply if suitable, leave when signed.

S1.quote: Customers should not have to fight a machine and then find nobody paid to check it.
fieldNote: The **five agents** make shared demands about paid time, authority and hours.
Her **quality examples** are de-identified before group discussion.
A job change requires **full-week written terms**, not a specialist label.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say a bot might issue the first refusal while a customer is still looking for the photograph it missed. I would ask five agents including me to sign one request for paid appeal-review time, clear authority to reopen a wrong refusal, and written weekly rotas. Customers should not have to fight a machine and then find nobody paid to check it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I think management may cut my team’s paid hours as routine claim chats move away. I am quick with the approved tools, but speed is not a guarantee of a full week. Five months saved and some nearby centres give us choices, not a reason to accept an invisible pay cut.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I would bring four de-identified wrong-refusal cases from our permitted quality log to the five-agent meeting. We would send the signed request for paid review time, reopening authority and written weekly rotas to our manager. I would keep working paid appeals; if my written hours fall, I would compare posted paid service-desk jobs by full weekly wages and hours after bus fare before applying.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about my own paid week shrinking. The group request is useful because all five of us see the same errors, but it does not make the manager agree. I can act now without pretending the reserve is permanent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the others actually join that request, and what would you share?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: There are five signers including me, not five people speaking on my behalf. We would each bring one example but send one request about our shared paid hours and authority. We would not put customer names in it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you apply for any role labelled claims specialist?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I would not leave because a vacancy says “claims specialist” in large type. I would need written full-week wages and hours that cover rent and utilities after the fare, and I would keep paid appeals until a suitable offer is signed. Some nearby centres does not mean every opening pays enough.

Cancel **paid cinema membership** only once most appeal hours actually end, stretching existing savings.
feel: I feel **anxious** about losing most paid hours despite several months to search.
S2.quote: The next full-week offer, rather than my confidence with a tool, would decide how safe we are.
fieldNote: The **membership cut** follows actual loss of most appeal hours, not a date alone.
She distinguishes **existing savings** from ongoing income.
She asks about **reopening authority** but makes written full-week pay and signed offer the hard gates.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell Emil full AGI by 2028 could read a policy, photograph and repair report before the appeals queue even forms. Robots visiting kitchens around 2031 are later; our call decisions are exposed first. I would want written dates for paid appeal shifts, not an assurance that good agents are valued.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think the centre could end most of our appeal hours, mine included. Five months saved is a serious cushion, but losing a full wage would start using it immediately. Emil’s florist wage would not carry rent and utilities by itself, and some nearby centres may be using the same system.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting in 2026 I would compare the last eight weekly payslips with rent, utilities and bus fares. If most paid appeals hours end after 2028, I would apply for posted paid service or claims desks only where written weekly wages and hours cover those costs after travel. I would keep any remaining paid appeals until a suitable offer is signed, and cancel our paid cinema membership once the hours actually fall to stretch the existing reserve.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about a sharp loss, though I can search for several months. I am not counting on every contact centre to keep its appeal team. The next full-week offer, rather than my confidence with a tool, would decide how safe we are.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you cut that membership now, before the hours change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I would not cancel the cinema membership merely because the card says 2028. I would do it if most paid appeal hours actually end. The five months are existing savings, not a fresh monthly income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would a job title or hourly figure be enough to switch?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would apply while I still have any paid shifts, but I would not accept or leave on an hourly number alone. The written full-week wages and hours must cover rent, utilities and fare; then the offer must be signed. I would ask who can reopen a claim, but I would weigh that answer rather than make it a hard job condition.

steps.text: Compare eight weekly payslips with rent, utilities and fares in 2026
Apply if most paid hours end post-2028: posted paid desk, written rent/utility-covering weekly pay/hours after fare
Keep remaining paid appeals until suitable offer is signed
Cancel paid cinema membership only after most paid appeal hours end

Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say five years is enough time to show which rejected claims are overturned when a missing repair photograph is found. Thinking AGI could change appeals by 2031; robots going into kitchens would follow around 2034. I would rather learn the rules of a paid loss-assessment desk than defend a queue that may be gone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my diploma and appeals record could transfer to a loss-assessment office, but I cannot call that a job until an opening is posted. My daily AI use helps me learn a new case system, yet a different policy book takes proper training. Five months saved lets me choose carefully; it does not pay a course fee and my wage at the same time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I would apply to a posted paid junior loss-assessment role if its written weekly wage and hours cover rent, utilities and fare. If that role requires the insurer’s two-week assessment course and the employer pays both the course fee and my time to attend, I would take it and learn the site-report rules. I would keep paid appeal shifts until a suitable offer is signed; if that posting disappears or my hours fall around 2031, I would check other posted paid claims desks with the same weekly cost test.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about the appeals rota but less trapped than in the fast case. Five years gives me time to see a real job description and train for it while paid. It does not guarantee that the loss-assessment office will hire me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take that course before there is a paid role?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would not buy the course on speculation. It belongs to a paid posted role that requires it, with the fees covered and attendance paid separately. If either is missing, I stay on paid appeals and check other vacancies.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would any loss-assessment title make you accept?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would take the first bus to a site only if the job actually includes visits and the shift and fare fit our numbers. I would ask who signs off a damage estimate before accepting, because a title alone does not tell me what I can decide. The written full week and signed offer remain the conditions for leaving.

Check posted paid desks if role fails or 2031 cuts: written rent/utility-covering weekly pay/hours after fare

Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell Emil a decade lets us compare actual pay and rent rather than pin a retirement date to 2036. Thinking AI could handle claim decisions then; kitchen robots are a later question around 2039. I would keep doing paid appeals while they are there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I might still want this wage at 68, and I do not know what income will replace it. Five months saved is useful but not a decade’s spending. I would like to teach younger agents how to read a repair report, provided we are both paid for the time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Each year I would compare our actual wages, rent, utilities, travel and any confirmed retirement income. I would keep the paid appeals rota and coach one newer agent on policy and repair reports during paid shifts. If my hours fall after 2036 and we still need my wage, I would compare posted paid claims desks by written weekly wages and hours covering rent and utilities after fare, and leave only on a suitable signed offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm about the longer planning time, though I would not call future income settled. Paid work and five months saved give us some room now. I would rather teach someone to spot the missing photograph than plan a farewell party with no numbers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you set a retirement date now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I would not promise Emil a retirement date based on the AGI year. We would need confirmed income that covers our bills at that time. If the figures do not work, I keep earning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would coaching a newer agent be extra unpaid work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would coach on paid time using real permitted cases with customer names removed. That is normal lead work, not a second job or a new course. If appeals paid hours fall, the written weekly offer and travel cost still decide whether I move.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because most appeal hours might end before a new full-week role opens. Five months saved buys a search, but Emil and I still have monthly rent and utilities. Written paid dates at the centre and a posted paid assessment opening with clear weekly terms would help me choose.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You did not ask who tells a customer that a refused fridge claim was wrong after the missing photograph turns up. A fast first answer is less valuable than a named person who can reopen the claim.

headlineQuote: A fast first answer is less valuable than a named person who can reopen the claim.
